title: AI Issuers Are Upending Longstanding Safety Valve
source_used: Business Standard (carrying the Bloomberg Credit Weekly article by Tasos Vossos)
key_facts: Big tech companies known as hyperscalers are willing to pay higher yields because they are borrowing to fund AI investments such as data centers and AI chips.
For a decade through 2025, high-grade debt sales fell when borrowing costs rose; this year the relationship has flipped, with yields and new bond supply rising together.
Companies have sold $1.69 trillion of US corporate bonds this year, up about 30% from a year earlier, while average yields rose about 1.2 percentage points to 5.97% as of Thursday's close.
Barclays' Scott Schulte expects hyperscaler capital spending of around $1 trillion next year, so AI bond issuance 'isn't going to slow down'; investors worry the market cannot absorb the supply.

Bloomberg and other outlets reported SpaceX is in talks to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips and Broadcom is sketching another large financing for OpenAI chips, after starting a $60 billion package that benefits Anthropic and others.
For most other companies rising yields slow issuance: US corporations sold only $11.4 billion of notes this week against $25 billion to $30 billion expected; European sales were EUR 16.2 billion.
Yields are rising for several reasons: AI financing, heavier government borrowing and inflation fears from the US-Iran standoff.
MUFG's Antoine Baudron said some transactions have not launched because of 'sticker shock'.
quote_evidence: Companies have sold $1.69 trillion of US corporate bonds this year, up about 30% from the same time last year, while average yields this year have risen about 1.2 percentage point to 5.97% as of Thursday's close.
For most other companies, rising yields will slow down issuance, as evident this week.
In addition to corporate financing for AI, governments are borrowing more, and inflation fears have grown in recent months as the standoff between the US and Iran persists.
why_it_matters_hint: A steady flow of AI borrowing keeps adding to bond supply even as yields rise, which is unusual and weighs on other issuers.
event_date: Weekly credit column of 10 Oct 2026; data to 8 Oct 2026
